newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - Ex-Nazi slaves pin hopes on compensation ruling.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Ex-Nazi slaves pin hopes on compensation ruling.

text.p: Roman Halter is still haunted by his time as a slave labourer in Hitler's arms factories over 50 years ago. As a Jew, he was "earmarked" for death and owes his survival to a string of random occurrences.

"It comes back to me in dreams that wake me in the night. I dream I'm on a roof cornered by the SS and don't know whether to jump," said Halter, speaking from his home in Britain. "Its an injury to one's spirit and mind that never goes away."
Now 69, Halter, a retired architect, says the older he gets and the more time he has to reflect, the more powerfully the trauma comes back to haunt him.
Halter is one of a group of about 150 former Nazi slaves living in Britain who launched a campaign last December to secure remuneration for their unpaid work and an apology from Germany.

They and similar groups in Israel, the United States and Canada are pinning their hopes on a five-year civil case in a Bonn court which will decide whether 21 Jewish women are entitled to such compensation from the German government.
The verdict, postponed from the end of January until spring, could pave the way for a flood of compensation claims.
Halter met one of the claimants, and, when he heard about her case, rallied other ex-slaves in Britain to follow suit.
"She has a list of 300 more former slave labourers in Israel who are keen to see the outcome of the case and we also know of about 100 similar people in the U.S. and Canada."
DEMANDS PRESENTED TO AMBASSADOR IN LONDON
Halter and his group, called Claims for Jewish Slave Labour Compensation, presented their demands in December to the German ambassador in London, Juergen Oesterhelt.
"If Germany wants to be an equal among democratic nations, it should recognise what is due to us, the compensation for the slave labour and a very nice apology," Halter said.
"It's not such a big thing for the German government, particularly when the SS, who were there to torture and kill us, are receiving pensions," he said.

"But we are worried the Germans are waiting for the biological solution, that if they create enough legal obstacles we will all be dead before they have to pay," he said. "This must be put right very quickly. We are all around 70."
The German government has declined comment on the Bonn case while it is in progress. But the claimants' representative in Germany, Baron Klaus von Muenchhausen, said he was optimistic.
"Its not a matter of if, but how much," said Muenchhausen, who represents women now living in Israel, the United States, Canada and Australia.
THE NAZI PAST OF GERMAN COMPANIES

The issue of slave labour during the Third Reich surfaced embarrassingly for German carmaker Volkswagen late last year when a new company history was published, revealing its unscrupulous use of slaves to build cars and armaments.

It described then VW founder Ferdinand Porsche as a "morally indifferent" Nazi and said he and war-time company chief, his son-in-law Anton Piech, were largely responsible for the treatment of thousands of slaves.

The book was sponsored by the company in an attempt to come clean about its Nazi past. Like VW, many German firms used slave labour during the war. Afterwards they argued they were forced to because of labour shortages.
Some still exist today or have legal successors, such as IG Farben which was divided into Germany's three biggest chemicals firms, Bayer, Hoechst and BASF.
SLAVES IN CAMPS FROM NORWAY TO ALGERIA

Hitler's armaments minister Albert Speer acknowledged 11 million slaves in 1944 -- seven million in Germany -- toiling in his vast empire of camps and arms factories stretching across the Nazi-occupied lands from Norway to Algeria.

The average lifespan of a Jewish slave labourer was three months and there are some estimates that as many of 90 percent died, Halter said, citing historians. An estimated 10,000 to 15,000 are still alive today, Holocaust experts say.

As a boy growing up in a town in northwest Poland, Halter's childhood came to an abrupt end in 1939 when the German army marched in and carried out pogroms that wiped out some of his immediate family.

A year later he and the remaining members of his family were sent to the Lodz Ghetto. After the notorious "selections" when deportees were picked to join an army of slaves, the SS who ran Hitler's concentration camps put Halter to work in a factory making metal accessories for the Germany army.
"We were on starvation rations. But as a factory worker I got a bowl of soup for lunch on top that," Halter said.
By 1943 he was the only member of his family still alive.

"The Jews were considered slave labour. We differed from POWs and others because we were earmarked for 'extermination through work' as (head of the Gestapo Heinrich) Himmler once said in a speech," Halter said.
"We had a death sentence over our heads. We knew we were going to die. It was only a matter of how long we would last. They tortured us, beat us and could murder us with impunity."
"I only survived because I became a skilled metalworker and was useful to the Reich."

In 1944 Halter was taken to Auschwitz, where he narrowly escaped death in the gas chambers. He worked on dismantling a factory in Poland as the Germans retreated from the advancing Red Army and finally constructed bullet tips in a factory near Dresden.
STRUGGLE FOR COMPENSATION
Despite their terrible plight, there has only been one successful suit for compensation by Nazi-era slave labourers.

IG Farben, which produced Zyklon B gas for the death camps, paid the Jewish Claims Conference 30 million marks in 1957 after a long and bitter campaign. But isolated claims have failed because of a number of legal snags.

Bonn has said it has paid 100 billion marks to compensate Nazi victims. But although slave labourers are legally entitled to compensation, they have failed to make successful claims in the past because of international agreements.
These stated that such payments could not be made until Germany concluded a peace treaty at the end of World War Two -- something that never actually happened during the Cold War.
Only since German unification in 1990 and a series of recent international treaties has the situation changed.
